properties.description:
On November 22, 2026, as part of a latest platform update, Microsoft turned off username and password sign-in to the Azure API Management Developer Portal due to inactivity. On those instances, developers can't sign in or sign up with a username and password. API traffic isn't affected.

What you need to do:

  • Recommended: set up Microsoft Entra ID for Developer Portal sign-in. 
  • Secure access to developer portal - Azure API Management | Microsoft Learn
  • To turn username and password sign-in back on: in the Azure portal, open your API Management instance and go to Developer portal > Identities > + Add > Username and password.
  • Set up Basic Authentication to the Developer Portal - Azure API Management | Microsoft Learn

properties.description:
What happened?

Between 14:38 UTC and 18:58 UTC on 27 October 2026, a subset of customers experienced connection failures, increased latency, failed requests, and failures performing management operations for services in the West Europe region. This impact began when a power failure in one of the datacenters supporting physical Availability Zone (AZ-01) caused a portion of the datacenter to lose power. Impacted services included:

  • Azure Database for MySQL Flexible Server: Customers experienced connection failures, and some servers were unavailable. Servers configured for zone redundancy were not affected. During recovery, servers took varying lengths of time to recover because each server first had to complete its own database recovery after its virtual machine recovered.
  • Azure SQL Database: Customers experienced connection failures and unavailability, including for some zone-redundant databases. Management operations also failed, as requests for server and database details timed out or returned errors, and creating, deleting, renaming, or changing the service tier of servers and databases did not complete.
  • Azure Storage: Azure Files, Azure Blob Storage (specifically block blobs) and Azure Data Lake Storage were impacted. Customers with affected storage accounts experienced failed or slow requests and reduced availability.
  • Azure Virtual Machines: Customers experienced VMs becoming unavailable or restarting unexpectedly, and management operations for those virtual machines may have been delayed or failed.

The impact of this event was confined to a portion of a single physical availability zone (AZ-01). However, the 'logical' availability zones used by each customer subscription may correspond to different physical availability zones. Customers can use the Locations API to understand this mapping and to confirm which resources run in this physical AZ: https://learn.microsoft.com/rest/api/resources/subscriptions/list-locations#availabilityzonemappings


The actions described here represent our initial investigation of the datacenter incident. By 4 December 2026, we will provide an update after the detailed investigation completes to provide more insights on the power infrastructure failures and specific actions we are taking to improve moving forward.

What went wrong, and why?

Azure datacenters are designed with multiple layers of electrical redundancy intended to maintain power to critical infrastructure when the primary utility supply is interrupted. When utility power is lost, uninterruptible power supply (UPS) systems across multiple sections of the datacenter maintain power on battery while backup generators start and assume the electrical load. This arrangement is designed to prevent an interruption to Azure services if utility power is lost.

During this incident, some elements of these protections did not perform as designed. At 14:33 UTC, a utility power disturbance interrupted the power supply to the datacenter. At that time, 21 of the 24 backup systems operated as designed, with UPS systems taking on the load before transferring it to backup generators. However, in the remaining three, we saw three distinct issues:

  • Automatic transfer switch (ATS) failure: In the first system, the automatic transfer switch, a device that moves the load from utility power to generator power, failed.
  • Battery thermal runaway: In the second system, the UPS batteries went into thermal runaway, a condition where a battery's rising temperature causes it to generate even more heat. The batteries could not support the load, and power was not restored until engineers manually switched the UPS to bypass mode, routing power around it.
  • UPS overvoltage: In the third system, an overvoltage condition stopped the UPS batteries from supporting the load. The UPS restarted automatically after about one minute and then transferred the load to the generator.

The server racks supplied by these three systems lost power and became unavailable. The rest of the datacenter remained powered throughout the event. The underlying causes for these three issues remain under close investigation.

The thermal runaway set off the smoke detection and gas suppression systems. Following our safety procedures, the site was fully evacuated and emergency services were called. Onsite recovery was paused while emergency services assessed the site, and resumed once they confirmed it was safe and gave the all-clear to re-enter.

The loss of power affected several layers of Azure infrastructure. Network devices lost power and connectivity, interrupting communication between parts of the affected infrastructure. Compute hosts became unavailable, affecting the virtual machines running on them, while storage infrastructure experienced connectivity and availability issues. These failures also affected dependent Azure services, including SQL Database and MySQL Flexible Server, which rely on the underlying network, compute, and storage infrastructure.

Our automated monitoring detected infrastructure and service-health degradation shortly after the disturbance began. Our engineering teams began investigating the electrical failure and its effects across the affected services, while datacenter personnel focused on restoring stable electrical power.

Network devices came back online automatically as power was restored to their racks.

Once all power was restored, we assessed the affected infrastructure and began recovering components that did not restart or reconnect automatically.

Restoring electrical power did not immediately restore every affected Azure service. Some components required additional investigation and recovery work. For example, one affected Azure Storage cluster remained unable to receive traffic for a period after its power and networking had recovered, until a load-balancing component for that cluster was returned to service. Similarly, affected compute hosts and virtual machines needed additional time to recover. Individual Azure service teams continued investigating and validating their services before confirming that customer operations had returned to normal.

Azure SQL Database databases that were not configured for zone redundancy recovered once power was restored. However, some zone-redundant databases were also affected. When their own nodes failed, they moved automatically to healthy nodes as designed, but some could not connect to their backing storage immediately. No zone-redundant Azure Database for MySQL Flexible Server resources were affected.

How did we respond?

  • 14:33 UTC on 27 October 2026 – Utility power to the datacenter was interrupted. 21 of the 24 backup power systems took over the load as designed, but three did not, due to an automatic transfer switch failure, a battery thermal runaway, and a UPS overvoltage.
  • 14:34 UTC on 27 October 2026 – Smoke detection and gas suppression systems triggered a site-wide evacuation, and emergency services were dispatched. Onsite recovery work was paused until the site was assessed and cleared for re-entry.
  • 14:38 UTC on 27 October 2026 – Racks supplied by the three affected backup power systems lost power, and customer impact began.
  • 14:41 UTC on 27 October 2026 – Automated monitoring detected the issue, and engineers began investigating.
  • 15:25 UTC on 27 October 2026 – Following a precautionary evacuation due to a smoke condition, local emergency services gave the site clear for phased safe re-entry, allowing datacenter staff to resume on-site recovery activities.
  • 15:57 UTC on 27 October 2026 – Datacenter staff began inspecting the affected areas onsite. Over the course of the next hour, generators were brought online progressively, to restore power to affected racks.
  • 16:09 UTC on 27 October 2026 – Power was restored to all affected racks.
  • 16:17 UTC on 27 October 2026 – As racks began to receive generator power, we confirmed that all affected network devices were back online.
  • 16:18 UTC on 27 October 2026 – Engineers restored the storage cluster's load-balancing component, and storage traffic began to return.
  • 16:19 UTC on 27 October 2026 – All affected virtual machines had recovered.
  • 16:20 UTC on 27 October 2026 – Power to all affected racks was stabilized, with generator power fully restored.
  • 16:23 UTC on 27 October 2026 – Azure SQL Database management operations recovered.
  • 16:39 UTC on 27 October 2026 – Network connectivity was confirmed healthy, and Azure Storage recovered fully.
  • 17:00 UTC on 27 October 2026 – Azure SQL Database connections recovered.
  • 18:02 UTC on 27 October 2026 – The virtual machines underlying Azure Database for MySQL Flexible Server had recovered. Each server then had to complete its own database recovery before it could accept connections again, and the time this took varied with each server's workload.
  • 18:58 UTC on 27 October 2026 – Customer impact was fully mitigated. The last Azure Database for MySQL Flexible Server servers completed database recovery, so all affected services were confirmed recovered.
  • 19:09 UTC on 28 October 2026 – The datacenter, which had remained on generator power with continuous fuel management since 27 October, returned to utility power after all affected UPS batteries had been replaced and every affected rack had been inspected.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

  • Replacement of affected UPS batteries: We replaced the UPS batteries affected by this event before returning the datacenter to utility power. (Completed)
  • Inspection of affected racks: We inspected every rack that lost power to confirm it was safe to return to normal operation. (Completed)
  • Investigation of the backup power performance: We are completing a detailed investigation into the underlying causes for the backup power infrastructure failing to perform as designed, including the ATS failure and the UPS thermal runaway, to identify further corrective and preventive actions for the datacenter's power systems. (Estimated completion: November 2026)


The actions described here represent our initial investigation of the datacenter incident. By 4 December 2026, we will provide an update after the detailed investigation completes to provide more insights on the power infrastructure failures and specific actions we are taking to improve moving forward.

How can customers make incidents like this less impactful?

  • This event affected infrastructure within a single availability zone. Zone-redundant resources are designed to remain available when one zone loses power, while resources deployed to a single zone, or configured without zone redundancy, can be affected by that zone's failure. For critical workloads, consider zone-redundant deployments: https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/reliability/availability-zones-overview and https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/reliability/availability-zones-zonal-resource-resiliency
  • Service-specific zone redundancy options are available for Azure SQL Database (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/azure-sql/database/high-availability-sla-local-zone-redundancy), Azure Database for MySQL Flexible Server (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/mysql/flexible-server/concepts-high-availability), and Azure Storage (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/storage/common/storage-redundancy).
  • More generally, consider evaluating the reliability of your applications using guidance from the Azure Well-Architected Framework and its interactive Well-Architected Review: https://aka.ms/AzPIR/WAF
  • The impact times represent the full incident duration, so are not specific to any individual customer. Actual impact to service availability varied between customers and resources. For guidance on implementing monitoring to understand granular impact: https://aka.ms/AzPIR/Monitoring
  • Finally, consider ensuring that the right people in your organization will be notified about any future service issues by configuring Azure Service Health alerts. These can trigger emails, SMS, push notifications, webhooks, and more: https://aka.ms/AzPIR/Alerts

How can we make our incident communications more useful?

What happened?

Between 14:38 UTC and 18:58 UTC on 27 October 2026, a subset of customers experienced connection failures, increased latency, failed requests, and failures performing management operations for services in the West Europe region. This impact began when a power failure in one of the datacenters supporting physical Availability Zone (AZ-01) caused a portion of the datacenter to lose power. Impacted services included:

  • Azure Database for MySQL Flexible Server: Customers experienced connection failures, and some servers were unavailable. Servers configured for zone redundancy were not affected. During recovery, servers took varying lengths of time to recover because each server first had to complete its own database recovery after its virtual machine recovered.
  • Azure SQL Database: Customers experienced connection failures and unavailability, including for some zone-redundant databases. Management operations also failed, as requests for server and database details timed out or returned errors, and creating, deleting, renaming, or changing the service tier of servers and databases did not complete.
  • Azure Storage: Azure Files, Azure Blob Storage (specifically block blobs) and Azure Data Lake Storage were impacted. Customers with affected storage accounts experienced failed or slow requests and reduced availability.
  • Azure Virtual Machines: Customers experienced VMs becoming unavailable or restarting unexpectedly, and management operations for those virtual machines may have been delayed or failed.

The impact of this event was confined to a portion of a single physical availability zone (AZ-01). However, the 'logical' availability zones used by each customer subscription may correspond to different physical availability zones. Customers can use the Locations API to understand this mapping and to confirm which resources run in this physical AZ: https://learn.microsoft.com/rest/api/resources/subscriptions/list-locations#availabilityzonemappings


The actions described here represent our initial investigation of the datacenter incident. By 4 December 2026, we will provide an update after the detailed investigation completes to provide more insights on the power infrastructure failures and specific actions we are taking to improve moving forward.

What went wrong, and why?

Azure datacenters are designed with multiple layers of electrical redundancy intended to maintain power to critical infrastructure when the primary utility supply is interrupted. When utility power is lost, uninterruptible power supply (UPS) systems across multiple sections of the datacenter maintain power on battery while backup generators start and assume the electrical load. This arrangement is designed to prevent an interruption to Azure services if utility power is lost.

During this incident, some elements of these protections did not perform as designed. At 14:33 UTC, a utility power disturbance interrupted the power supply to the datacenter. At that time, 21 of the 24 backup systems operated as designed, with UPS systems taking on the load before transferring it to backup generators. However, in the remaining three, we saw three distinct issues:

  • Automatic transfer switch (ATS) failure: In the first system, the automatic transfer switch, a device that moves the load from utility power to generator power, failed.
  • Battery thermal runaway: In the second system, the UPS batteries went into thermal runaway, a condition where a battery's rising temperature causes it to generate even more heat. The batteries could not support the load, and power was not restored until engineers manually switched the UPS to bypass mode, routing power around it.
  • UPS overvoltage: In the third system, an overvoltage condition stopped the UPS batteries from supporting the load. The UPS restarted automatically after about one minute and then transferred the load to the generator.

The server racks supplied by these three systems lost power and became unavailable. The rest of the datacenter remained powered throughout the event. The underlying causes for these three issues remain under close investigation.

The thermal runaway set off the smoke detection and gas suppression systems. Following our safety procedures, the site was fully evacuated and emergency services were called. Onsite recovery was paused while emergency services assessed the site, and resumed once they confirmed it was safe and gave the all-clear to re-enter.

The loss of power affected several layers of Azure infrastructure. Network devices lost power and connectivity, interrupting communication between parts of the affected infrastructure. Compute hosts became unavailable, affecting the virtual machines running on them, while storage infrastructure experienced connectivity and availability issues. These failures also affected dependent Azure services, including SQL Database and MySQL Flexible Server, which rely on the underlying network, compute, and storage infrastructure.

Our automated monitoring detected infrastructure and service-health degradation shortly after the disturbance began. Our engineering teams began investigating the electrical failure and its effects across the affected services, while datacenter personnel focused on restoring stable electrical power.

Network devices came back online automatically as power was restored to their racks.

Once all power was restored, we assessed the affected infrastructure and began recovering components that did not restart or reconnect automatically.

Restoring electrical power did not immediately restore every affected Azure service. Some components required additional investigation and recovery work. For example, one affected Azure Storage cluster remained unable to receive traffic for a period after its power and networking had recovered, until a load-balancing component for that cluster was returned to service. Similarly, affected compute hosts and virtual machines needed additional time to recover. Individual Azure service teams continued investigating and validating their services before confirming that customer operations had returned to normal.

Azure SQL Database databases that were not configured for zone redundancy recovered once power was restored. However, some zone-redundant databases were also affected.   • 14:41 UTC on 27 October 2026 – Automated monitoring detected the issue, and engineers began investigating.
  • 15:25 UTC on 27 October 2026 – Following a precautionary evacuation due to a smoke condition, local emergency services gave the site clear for phased safe re-entry, allowing datacenter staff to resume on-site recovery activities.
  • 15:57 UTC on 27 October 2026 – Datacenter staff began inspecting the affected areas onsite. Over the course of the next hour, generators were brought online progressively, to restore power to affected racks.
  • 16:09 UTC on 27 October 2026 – Power was restored to all affected racks.
  • 16:17 UTC on 27 October 2026 – As racks began to receive generator power, we confirmed that all affected network devices were back online.
  • 16:18 UTC on 27 October 2026 – Engineers restored the storage cluster's load-balancing component, and storage traffic began to return.
  • 16:19 UTC on 27 October 2026 – All affected virtual machines had recovered.
  • 16:20 UTC on 27 October 2026 – Power to all affected racks was stabilized, with generator power fully restored.
  • 16:23 UTC on 27 October 2026 – Azure SQL Database management operations recovered.
  • 16:39 UTC on 27 October 2026 – Network connectivity was confirmed healthy, and Azure Storage recovered fully.
  • 17:00 UTC on 27 October 2026 – Azure SQL Database connections recovered.

  • 18:58 UTC on 27 October 2026 – Customer impact was fully mitigated. The last Azure Database for MySQL Flexible Server servers completed database recovery, so all affected services were confirmed recovered.

  • UPS overvoltage: In the third system, an overvoltage condition stopped the UPS batteries from supporting the load. The UPS restarted automatically after about one minute and then transferred the load to the generator.

On November 22, 2026, as part of a latest platform update, Microsoft turned off username and password sign-in to the Azure API Management Developer Portal due to inactivity. On those instances, developers can't sign in or sign up with a username and password. API traffic isn't affected.

What you need to do:

  • Recommended: set up Microsoft Entra ID for Developer Portal sign-in. 
  • Secure access to developer portal - Azure API Management | Microsoft Learn
  • To turn username and password sign-in back on: in the Azure portal, open your API Management instance and go to Developer portal > Identities > + Add > Username and password.
  • Set up Basic Authentication to the Developer Portal - Azure API Management | Microsoft Learn
